c11_acc_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c11_acc_ch01.scenario: You volunteer as treasurer for your school's two-day cultural fest. On day one: a sponsor pays ₹20,000, you hire a popular band for day two, the principal announces a donation, and a stall's fridge breaks down (₹8,000 repair estimate). Back in the accounts room, a teammate says every announcement should go in the books because they are all important.
c11_acc_ch01.prompt: Which events actually enter the fest's accounts?

options.text: Record the sponsor's ₹20,000 and the fridge loss estimate — both are economic events measurable in money. The band hiring becomes a transaction only when the service/payment is made, and the principal's announcement is not measurable until the money is promised in writing and received.
options.outcome: Accounting filters events through monetary measurability: only what can be expressed in rupees is recorded, however 'important' the rest feels.

options.text: Record all four — the band booking and the announced donation are significant events for the fest.
options.outcome: Significance is not the test; without a monetary amount attached to an exchange, the event stays outside the books.

options.text: Just write down whatever cash physically moved today — accounting is only cash in and cash out.
options.outcome: That reduces accounting to book-keeping of cash; accounting records all measurable economic events (including credit and losses) and then analyses them for decisions.

c11_acc_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c11_acc_ch02.scenario: During a school entrepreneurship project you must pick one of two neighbourhood juice carts to 'invest' the club's ₹50,000 in. Cart A reports ₹80,000 profit — but counts only cash actually collected. Cart B reports ₹60,000 — counting all sales made, including ₹15,000 still owed by regulars. A teammate says: pick Cart A, the bigger profit wins.
c11_acc_ch02.prompt: What is the right way to compare the two carts?

options.text: You cannot compare them yet — first restate both profits on the same basis (accrual, per GAAP). Cart A's cash-basis profit understates what it earned; only common rules make the numbers comparable.
options.outcome: GAAP exists precisely so that 'profit' means the same thing for every business; comparisons across firms demand a shared framework, not the bigger raw number.

options.text: Pick Cart A — a business is free to keep books however it likes, and ₹80,000 is the better figure.
options.outcome: Without uniform principles each business speaks a private language; Cart A's cash-basis figure and Cart B's accrual figure answer different questions.

options.text: Check which cart followed GAAP as laid down in the Companies Act — whichever broke the law is disqualified.
options.outcome: GAAP is not a statute; it is a professional framework of concepts, conventions and standards. Small carts are not 'illegal' for lacking it — their figures are just not comparable.

c11_acc_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c11_acc_ch03.scenario: Interning at your uncle's electronics shop, you're asked to enter the day's transactions. The counter boy says: 'Sold a phone for ₹14,000 cash to a walk-in — no bill was printed, but I remember it. Also, uncle took ₹2,000 from the till for his daughter's school fees. And a supplier delivered ₹30,000 of stock on credit — the invoice is in the drawer.'
c11_acc_ch03.prompt: What do you record, and on what evidence?

options.text: Record the cash sale by issuing a cash memo now (no source document, no entry), the supplier's credit purchase from the invoice, and uncle's ₹2,000 as drawings — a business transaction because it changes the firm's position.
options.outcome: Every entry needs a source document; and the owner's drawing changes the firm's capital even though it feels 'personal'.

options.text: Record the phone sale from the counter boy's memory — a transaction happened, so evidence is optional.
options.outcome: Memory is not verifiable evidence; without a source document the entry has no objective proof and the books can't be audited.

options.text: Skip uncle's ₹2,000 — it's his personal family expense, so it's not a business transaction.
options.outcome: The money came from the firm's till, so the firm's cash and capital both changed; drawings is a business transaction even though the purpose was personal.

c11_acc_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c11_acc_ch04.scenario: As treasurer of the school canteen co-op you keep a Simple Cash Book. Today's slip reads: 'Cash sales ₹3,400; paid for bread ₹900; sold 20 coupon books to Class 12 on credit ₹2,000 (they'll pay Monday); deposited ₹1,500 of the cash into the co-op's bank account.' A junior member insists all four lines go on the cash book's receipts side.
c11_acc_ch04.prompt: What actually goes into the cash book, and where?

options.text: Debit side: cash sales ₹3,400. Credit side: bread payment ₹900. The bank deposit is a contra entry (cash out, bank in). The credit coupon sale is excluded entirely — no cash moved today.
options.outcome: The Simple Cash Book records only cash movements; the credit sale waits for Monday's cash, and the deposit touches both sides as a contra entry.

options.text: Record the ₹2,000 coupon sale as a receipt — a sale is a sale, and the money is as good as received.
options.outcome: Until cash actually moves, a credit sale has no place in a cash book; recording it inflates cash in hand that doesn't exist.

options.text: Show the bank deposit only once — as a payment — since cash physically left the drawer.
options.outcome: A deposit moves value between two accounts the business owns; it must appear on both sides as a contra entry or the bank record won't reconcile.

c11_acc_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c11_acc_ch05.scenario: You run a small online craft store after school. Your own cash book says the bank holds ₹18,600; the bank statement says ₹21,100. The gap traces to: a ₹3,000 cheque you issued to a supplier (not yet presented), a ₹700 bank charge you never recorded, and a ₹4,200 customer UPI that the bank credited but you forgot to enter. Your friend says the bank must have made an error.
c11_acc_ch05.prompt: How do you explain the difference?

options.text: These are timing differences and your own omissions, not necessarily bank error: starting from the pass book, deduct the unpresented cheque effect appropriately, adjust for the bank charge and the unrecorded credit to reconcile to ₹18,600.
options.outcome: A BRS works because you and the bank record the same events at different times; each item has a direction depending on which balance you start from.

options.text: Always add the differences to the cash book balance to reach the pass book balance — that's the rule.
options.outcome: Direction depends on the starting point and whether the item makes that balance higher or lower; a memorised 'always add' fails the moment you start from the other side.

options.text: The bank probably posted someone else's money to your account — file a complaint and wait.
options.outcome: Before blaming the bank, list every item and ask which book recorded it first; almost all gaps are timing differences or your own unrecorded items.

c11_acc_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c11_acc_ch06.scenario: At your internship, the senior accountant asks you to check the books of a client's café. You extract a trial balance: debits ₹4,86,000, credits ₹4,86,000 — it tallies. You email the client: 'Books are error-free, accounts can be finalised.' Hidden in the ledger: the new ₹90,000 espresso machine was debited to Purchases, and a ₹12,000 cash sale was never recorded at all.

options.text: No — the trial balance proves only arithmetical accuracy. The machine in Purchases is an error of principle and the missed sale is complete omission; both leave debits equal to credits while profit and assets are materially wrong.
options.outcome: Tallying columns can't see wrong account classification or missing transactions; the trial balance is a first check, not a certificate of truth.

options.text: Yes — equal totals mean every transaction was recorded correctly, that's the whole point of double entry.
options.outcome: Double entry guarantees equal debits and credits even when the wrong account is debited or a transaction is skipped entirely.

options.text: No — but the only error a trial balance can miss is a compensating one, where two mistakes cancel.
options.outcome: It also misses errors of principle, complete omission, and wrong subsidiary books; narrowing the blind spots to one type understates the problem.

c11_acc_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c11_acc_ch07.scenario: Your family's catering business bought a delivery van for ₹9 lakh (expected life 6 years, scrap ₹90,000). Used vans are suddenly in demand and your father says: 'The van's market value has actually gone up this year — charging depreciation would be silly. And anyway, no cash went out, so it's not a real expense.'
c11_acc_ch07.prompt: Should the business still charge depreciation?

options.text: Yes — depreciation allocates the van's historical cost (₹9 lakh minus scrap) over its useful life so each year's revenue bears the cost of using it; it is a non-cash expense driven by the matching principle, not a mark-to-market adjustment.
options.outcome: Skipping it overstates this year's profit and understates future years'; market value movements are irrelevant to cost allocation.

options.text: No — depreciation exists to write the asset down to market value, and the market value rose.
options.outcome: That confuses accounting depreciation (cost allocation) with economic depreciation (value change); the books charge the original cost regardless of resale prices.

options.text: No — since no cash left the business this year, there is nothing to record.
options.outcome: Expense ≠ cash outflow; the van's cost was 'consumed' helping earn this year's revenue, so a portion must be charged to match it.

c11_acc_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c11_acc_ch08.scenario: You're helping your aunt finalise her bakery's accounts for the bank loan application. In the expense pile: a new deck oven ₹4.5 lakh, a major ₹1.2 lakh overhaul that added five years to the old mixer, routine servicing ₹18,000, and ₹1.8 lakh advance rent for the next three years. The clerk put everything except the oven under 'expenses' because 'repairs and rent are never assets.'

options.text: The mixer overhaul is capital expenditure — it extends earning capacity beyond one period — and the advance rent is a prepaid asset, not this year's expense. Only the ₹18,000 servicing is pure revenue expenditure; the oven is capital.
options.outcome: The test is the period over which the benefit flows and whether earning capacity is increased or merely maintained — not the label 'repair' or the size of the payment.

options.text: The clerk is right — repairs maintain an asset and rent is a classic expense, so both stay in the P&L.
options.outcome: A life-extending overhaul increases earning capacity (capital), and three-year advance rent benefits future periods (prepaid asset); labels mislead, benefits decide.

options.text: Everything above ₹1 lakh is capital expenditure — the amounts decide.
options.outcome: Size is irrelevant; a huge payment that benefits only this period is revenue expenditure, and a small upgrade can be capital.

c11_acc_ch09.title: Use it in the wild
c11_acc_ch09.scenario: Your friend's tuition centre closes its books on 31 March. In July they paid ₹24,000 for a 12-month insurance policy; in March a corporate client signed up for a 10-month course paying ₹50,000 in advance, only one month of which falls in this year. Your friend says: 'Just put insurance and commission fully in this year's P&L — the cash moved this year, and adjustments are only for fixing mistakes anyway.'
c11_acc_ch09.prompt: How much of each belongs in this year's profit?

options.text: Insurance: 9 of 12 months = ₹18,000 to P&L, ₹6,000 prepaid to the balance sheet. Advance fee: 1 of 10 months = ₹5,000 to P&L, ₹45,000 unearned income as a liability. Adjustments aren't error-fixes — they apply accrual: recognise income when earned, expenses when incurred.
options.outcome: Every adjustment asks 'what belongs to this period?' — the rest goes to the balance sheet as an asset or liability.

options.text: Both fully in this year's P&L — cash moved this year, so the expense and income are this year's.
options.outcome: That's the cash basis; accrual matching sends the future-period share to the balance sheet, otherwise profit is distorted in both years.

options.text: Adjust the insurance (expenses need adjusting) but take the full ₹50,000 as income — income doesn't need adjustments.
options.outcome: The same accrual logic runs both ways: income received in advance is a liability until earned, exactly like prepaid expense is an asset until used.

c11_biotech_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c11_biotech_ch01.scenario: On a class field trip to a biotech park you visit three units: a unit making curd cultures and traditional fermented foods, a unit mass-producing penicillin from a Penicillium strain improved by decades of strain selection, and a unit making recombinant insulin in engineered E. coli. Your friend labels all three 'modern biotechnology' because all use microbes.

options.text: Only the recombinant insulin unit — modern biotechnology is defined by rDNA technology, i.e., deliberately cutting and rejoining DNA. The curd unit is ancient/classical fermentation and penicillin from a selected (not engineered) strain is classical, even though microbes are used.
options.outcome: The classifier is the technology, not the product: no constructed recombinant DNA means not modern biotechnology.

options.text: All three — biotechnology means using living organisms for products, and all three use microbes, so all are modern.
options.outcome: That erases the field's own history: ancient (domestication), classical (fermentation without genetic manipulation), modern (rDNA). Using a microbe is not the same as engineering its genome.

options.text: Only the penicillin and insulin units — fermentation of curd is too simple to count as biotechnology at all.
options.outcome: Dahi-making is the classical phase of biotechnology; excluding it shows the definition was memorised as 'high-tech only' rather than 'processing materials using living systems'.

c11_biotech_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c11_biotech_ch02.scenario: During a lab internship you're handed an electron micrograph of an unknown cell. You observe: a double-membrane nucleus with pores, mitochondria with cristae — and inside one organelle, 70S ribosomes. Your lab partner declares it prokaryotic: '70S ribosomes = prokaryote, textbook rule.'
c11_biotech_ch02.prompt: Prokaryote or eukaryote — and what settles it?

options.text: Eukaryote — a membrane-bound nucleus and mitochondria are decisive; the 70S ribosomes are inside chloroplasts/mitochondria, which is expected since those organelles carry their own prokaryote-type ribosomes. What matters is the cytoplasmic ribosome type (80S) plus a true nucleus.
options.outcome: Ribosome size must be read with location: organellar 70S ribosomes don't make a eukaryotic cell prokaryotic.

options.text: Prokaryote — 70S ribosomes are a standalone diagnostic marker; one feature is enough.
options.outcome: 70S ribosomes also live inside eukaryotic mitochondria and chloroplasts; classification rests on compartmentalisation (nucleus, organelles), not a single number.

options.text: Can't be decided — micrographs only show size, never internal structure.
options.outcome: Electron micrographs resolve membranes, cristae and nuclear pores precisely; refusing to read structural evidence abandons the actual diagnostic criteria.

c11_biotech_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c11_biotech_ch03.scenario: You're designing a 'high-fibre energy bar' for the school sports team and comparing two ingredient options: maltodextrin (short α-linked glucose chains, digested fast) versus cellulose fibre (β-1→4 linked glucose chains). A teammate argues both are 'just glucose chains', so they'll give identical energy — pick whichever is cheaper.
c11_biotech_ch03.prompt: Will the two glucose polymers deliver the same usable energy to the athletes?

options.text: No — human amylases and disaccharidases hydrolyse α-glycosidic linkages (maltodextrin → glucose → energy) but cannot break β-1→4 linkages in cellulose, so cellulose passes undigested as fibre. Same monomer, different linkage stereochemistry, opposite fates.
options.outcome: Glycosidic bond geometry, not the monomer, decides digestibility — cellulose adds bulk and gut benefit but no calories.

options.text: Yes — both are polysaccharides of glucose, so the body will extract the same glucose units either way.
options.outcome: Humans lack cellulase; the β-1→4 bonds survive digestion intact, so 'same sugar units' never reach the blood.

options.text: Cellulose gives MORE energy because its chain is longer — more glucose units means more calories.
options.outcome: Chain length is irrelevant when the bonds can't be cleaved; undigested polymer contributes zero metabolic energy however long it is.

c11_biotech_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c11_biotech_ch04.scenario: At a diagnostics company internship, your mentor asks you to file three newly characterised enzymes into IUB classes. One is named 'citrate synthase' (joins acetyl-CoA to oxaloacetate by transferring the acetyl group), another 'ATP citrate lyase' (a transferase despite its name), and a third needs EDTA-chelation testing because it dies without its Mg²⁺ cofactor. Your batchmate says: 'Just file by the name — synthase is a ligase, lyase is a lyase.'
c11_biotech_ch04.prompt: What's the correct way to classify them?

options.text: Classify by reaction chemistry, not the trivial name: citrate synthase is a transferase (acetyl group transfer), and any 'lyase' that moves groups is a transferase too. Separately, test cofactor dependence — without Mg²⁺ the apoenzyme is inactive; only apoenzyme + cofactor = catalytically active holoenzyme.
options.outcome: IUB classes are defined by the bond/group changes in the reaction; names routinely mislead (citrate synthase is EC 2.x, a transferase).

options.text: File by the name — the nomenclature exists precisely so the name tells you the class.
options.outcome: Trivial names encode history, not mechanism; 'synthase' and 'lyase' in names have trapped students into wrong classes — only the balanced reaction reveals the truth.

options.text: Skip the cofactor test — an enzyme is a protein catalyst, so the protein part alone defines its activity.
options.outcome: Many enzymes need metal ions or coenzymes; the apoenzyme without its cofactor is catalytically dead, so holoenzyme status is part of characterising it.

c11_biotech_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c11_biotech_ch05.scenario: You're assisting a college cancer-biology lab that is screening a new drug on cultured cells. You notice treated cells accumulate in G2 with damaged DNA and never enter mitosis, while untreated cells zip through. A junior says: 'The drug must act during M phase — interphase is just the resting stage anyway, nothing important happens there.'
c11_biotech_ch05.prompt: What's wrong with the junior's reasoning?

options.text: The drug likely works by triggering the G2/M checkpoint in response to DNA damage — and interphase is anything but resting: G1 builds mass and proteins, S replicates the entire genome, G2 verifies fidelity. Checkpoints sit inside interphase precisely because that's where the damage occurs and is detected.
options.outcome: Cell-cycle checkpoints are quality gates inside G1/S/G2; calling interphase 'resting' hides where regulation actually happens.

options.text: Agreed — all the interesting events are in mitosis; G1, S and G2 are just the cell idling between divisions.
options.outcome: In a 24-hour cycle M takes about an hour; the other 23 hours replicate 6 billion base pairs and build the mitotic machinery — the busiest part of the cycle.

options.text: The drug clearly acts in S phase — DNA damage can only happen while DNA is being copied.
options.outcome: DNA damage can arise in any phase (radiation, chemicals, stalled processes); the observed G2 accumulation points at the G2/M checkpoint checking replication fidelity, not at S phase itself.

c11_biotech_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c11_biotech_ch06.scenario: Your biology teacher wants the class to run a mini-Mendel project this year. Proposals on the table: ornamental roses, the school's mango tree, and fast-cycling Brassica (rapa) plants. A classmate votes for the mango tree 'because it's big and gives lots of fruit' and roses 'because they're pretty and common'.
c11_biotech_ch06.prompt: Which organism should the class pick, and on Mendel's actual criteria?

options.text: Fast-cycling Brassica: short generation time (weeks, not years), controllable pollination (bisexual flowers you can emasculate and hand-cross), discrete contrasting traits, many offspring per cross, and the ability to make true-breeding lines first — Mendel's real criteria were experimental control, not convenience or size.
options.outcome: Mendel chose peas because their biology kept the signal clean: pure lines, controlled crosses, countable discrete traits, big samples.

options.text: The mango tree — more seeds and fruit means more data, and that's all Mendel needed.
options.outcome: A mango takes years to flower and you can't control its pollination or get true-breeding lines in a school year; raw numbers without controlled parentage produce noise, not ratios.

options.text: Roses — Mendel picked peas simply because they were common in his garden, so any common plant works.
options.outcome: Commonness wasn't the point: peas self-pollinate unless you intervene, show discrete non-overlapping traits, and breed true — roses' hybridised, continuous traits would bury any 3:1 signal.

c11_biotech_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c11_biotech_ch07.scenario: At a vaccine-awareness talk, someone asks: 'How can an RNA virus like HIV end up inside our DNA? Doesn't the Central Dogma say information only goes DNA→RNA→Protein? That means HIV is breaking the laws of molecular biology!'
c11_biotech_ch07.prompt: Does reverse transcription violate the Central Dogma?

options.text: No — Crick's dogma forbids information flowing OUT of protein (Protein→DNA/RNA/Protein). RNA→DNA via reverse transcriptase was unknown in 1958 but never forbidden; it's an added pathway consistent with the rule that protein can't pass information back.
options.outcome: The dogma is about directionality of information flow, not a mandatory three-step pipeline; retroviruses extend the map without breaking it.

options.text: Yes — RNA→DNA is backwards, so HIV literally violates the Central Dogma.
options.outcome: The dogma never required the exact sequence DNA→RNA→Protein; it only banned protein as an information source. Reverse transcription is a legitimate extra arrow.

options.text: No violation because the virus converts RNA to protein directly — no DNA is ever made.
options.outcome: HIV does make a DNA copy (that's why it's a retrovirus and integrates into the genome); the defence is that RNA→DNA was always permitted, not that it doesn't happen.

c11_biotech_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c11_biotech_ch08.scenario: As a summer helper in a cytogenetics lab, you're asked to sort metaphase chromosome images. One chromosome shows a centromere at the very tip with a single visible arm. Your supervisor says: 'Good catch — check whether that's a human chromosome at all.'

options.text: Flag it as non-human or abnormal — no normal human chromosome is truly telocentric; even the smallest acrocentrics (13, 14, 15, 21, 22, Y) keep a tiny short arm with stalk and satellite. Measure the centromere index: CI = 0% means telocentric, which doesn't occur in a normal human karyotype.
options.outcome: Centromere position is the fixed landmark for classification; human acrocentrics are sub-terminal, never terminal.

options.text: Classify it as a normal telocentric human chromosome — the smallest chromosomes have their centromeres at the end.
options.outcome: That imports rodent/plant cytogenetics into humans; human chromosomes always retain a short p-arm, however small.

options.text: Classify by total length instead — the shortest chromosome must be chromosome 21.
options.outcome: Length alone doesn't fix identity; centromere position (metacentric/submetacentric/acrocentric) and arm ratio are the diagnostic features.

c11_biotech_ch09.title: Use it in the wild
c11_biotech_ch09.scenario: A cousin in medical college is analysing sequencing reads from a patient's tumour. She pastes one raw read into BLAST, gets a top hit, and declares the diagnosis done: 'Bioinformatics = BLAST, one tool, one answer.'
c11_biotech_ch09.prompt: Is one BLAST hit a diagnosis?

options.text: No — bioinformatics is a pipeline: raw reads → quality control (adapter/quality trimming) → alignment to reference → variant calling → annotation against curated databases → interpretation. Skipping QC or stopping at the first BLAST hit risks artifacts being read as mutations.
options.outcome: Each stage's output constrains the next; a single top hit without QC, alignment statistics and clinical annotation is not evidence.

options.text: Yes — BLAST searches the entire known database, so the top hit IS the answer.
options.outcome: BLAST is one tool in a multi-stage workflow; uncleaned reads and unverified variants make the 'top hit' meaningless for diagnosis.

options.text: No — she should instead download all known genomes and compare them manually to be thorough.
options.outcome: That replaces the pipeline with brute force; the field exists because petabyte-scale data needs indexed databases and staged algorithms, not manual reading.

c11_biotech_ch10.title: Use it in the wild
c11_biotech_ch10.scenario: For a school science project you want to compare the 3D structures of human and zebrafish insulin. Your partner says: 'Search CATH for the PDB file — a PDB ID maps straight to a CATH code, and PDB and CATH are basically the same database with different names.'
c11_biotech_ch10.prompt: How do you actually get structures and their classifications?

options.text: Retrieve the experimental structure files (coordinates, method, resolution) from PDB; then use CATH to see how each protein's domains are classified (Class→Architecture→Topology→Homology). One PDB entry can contain several CATH domains — they are complementary, not interchangeable.
options.outcome: PDB stores raw experimental entries; CATH organises individual domains into structural families — you need both, in that order.

options.text: One PDB ID gives one CATH code — just type the ID into CATH and read the answer.
options.outcome: CATH works at the domain level; multi-domain or multi-chain PDB entries split into several CATH domains, so there's no 1:1 mapping.

options.text: Skip PDB — CATH alone contains the coordinates, so it replaces PDB entirely.
options.outcome: CATH is a classification layer over experimental data; it doesn't host raw coordinate files, so you still need PDB for the structures themselves.

c11_biotech_ch11.title: Use it in the wild
c11_biotech_ch11.scenario: Your biology club downloads the 4.4-million-base-pair genome of M. tuberculosis as a text file to find all genes starting with ATG and compute GC content in sliding windows. Excel crashes. A member says: 'This is hopeless — bioinformatics programming means writing new algorithms in C, and none of us can do that.'
c11_biotech_ch11.prompt: What does the task actually require?

options.text: A short script using existing libraries — parse the FASTA, scan for ATG windows, compute GC% — a few dozen lines of Python with Biopython. Real bioinformatics practice is mostly parsing formats, gluing libraries and automating pipelines, not inventing algorithms.
options.outcome: The bottleneck was the biology question (what to look for), not algorithm design; scripting handles the data deluge that crashes Excel.

options.text: Agree it's hopeless — without algorithm-development skills, genome analysis can't be done by students.
options.outcome: That confuses computer-science research with bioinformatics practice; most daily work is data wrangling with off-the-shelf tools.

options.text: Split the file into 50 chunks and have each member search manually — teamwork replaces code.
options.outcome: Manual search across 4.4 million bases is error-prone and unreproducible; a script runs the same pattern search on any genome in seconds.

c11_biotech_ch12.title: Use it in the wild
c11_biotech_ch12.scenario: Your school lab gets three requests in one week: (a) image the 3D surface of a pollen grain, (b) visualise the internal membranes of a mitochondrion, (c) track a GFP-tagged protein moving in a living cell, and (d) see a 20 nm ribosome. A senior says: 'Use the compound light microscope at 1000× for everything — maximum zoom solves all of it.'

options.text: Pollen surface → SEM; mitochondrion interior → TEM; live GFP tracking → fluorescence/confocal. The ribosome is beyond light microscopy entirely: resolution is capped near ~200 nm by the wavelength of light, so 1000× magnification just enlarges blur — electrons' tiny wavelength is what resolves 20 nm.
options.outcome: Choose by resolution and sample question, not zoom: magnification without resolving power reveals nothing new.

options.text: The senior is right — 1000× is more than enough for ribosomes since bigger magnification shows smaller things.
options.outcome: Magnification spreads the image; resolution sets the smallest distinguishable detail. Light physically cannot resolve 20 nm objects, whatever the zoom.

options.text: Use TEM for everything including the living cell — highest resolution wins every time.
options.outcome: TEM needs fixed, sectioned, vacuum-compatible samples — a living cell dies in the beam; live tracking needs fluorescence microscopy even at lower resolution.

c11_bio_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bio_ch01.scenario: In a school debate on 'What is life?', your opponent argues fire is alive: it moves, grows by spreading, consumes oxygen, and produces 'offspring' sparks. She challenges you: 'Name one living characteristic fire lacks.'

options.text: Fire only mimics life at the surface: its 'respiration' is uncontrolled oxidation with no enzymes or ATP coupling, its 'growth' is thermal diffusion not cellular accretion, and its 'reproduction' is fragmentation with no genetic inheritance. Life is a syndrome — cellular organisation, metabolism, homeostasis, heredity — where each process runs through molecular machinery fire doesn't have.
options.outcome: Analogical resemblance is not homological equivalence: what matters is the mechanism underneath each characteristic.

options.text: Concede — fire shows movement, growth, energy use and reproduction, so by the checklist it's alive.
options.outcome: The checklist tests mechanism, not resemblance; fire fails every criterion once you ask how each process is carried out.

options.text: Fire isn't alive only because it can't move from place to place on its own — movement is the decisive test.
options.outcome: Movement alone is a weak criterion (streams move, rooted plants don't); the full syndrome of cellular, metabolic, hereditary traits is what defines life.

c11_bio_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bio_ch02.scenario: On a field trip your class collects pond water and finds three organisms: a bacterium with no nucleus, a green Euglena that photosynthesises but also ingests food and swims with a flagellum, and a slime mould that creeps over the log like an animal but fruits like a fungus. A classmate wants to force each into 'plant' or 'animal'.
c11_bio_ch02.prompt: Where do the three actually belong in Whittaker's system?

options.text: Bacterium → Monera (prokaryotic); Euglena and slime mould → Protista (unicellular eukaryotes). Whittaker's criteria — cell type, body organisation, nutrition mode — exist precisely because plant/animal can't absorb organisms like Euglena; and even Protista's boundaries are admittedly loose.
options.outcome: The five-kingdom system was invented for organisms that break the plant/animal binary; 'motile = animal' or 'green = plant' is the collapsed two-kingdom thinking.

options.text: Euglena is a plant because it's green and photosynthesises; the slime mould is an animal because it moves.
options.outcome: Single traits mislead — Euglena is also heterotrophic and motile, and slime moulds form spore-bearing fruiting bodies; Whittaker weighs cell type, organisation and nutrition together.

options.text: Protista is a natural kingdom of close relatives, so both Euglena and slime mould belong there permanently and comfortably.
options.outcome: NCERT itself warns Protista's boundaries are not well defined — it's a convenience grouping of single-celled eukaryotes, not a monophyletic clade.

c11_bio_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bio_ch03.scenario: Your eco-club is cataloguing plants on a trek: moss carpets on bark, ferns unfurling in the shade, a pine bearing cones, and a flowering mango. A teammate sorts them as 'cryptogams = simple plants without plumbing' and 'phanerogams = advanced plants with vascular tissue'.

options.text: The fern — a cryptogam (spore-bearing, no seed) that possesses full xylem and phloem, true roots, stems and leaves. Seedlessness is the cryptogam criterion, not absence of vascular tissue; evolution produced vessels before seeds, and seeds before flowers.
options.outcome: Cryptogam vs phanerogam is a reproductive split (spores vs seeds); vascular tissue and 'advanced' structure evolved on a different timeline.

options.text: The pine — it's 'lower' because it has no flowers, so it must be a cryptogam like the moss.
options.outcome: Gymnosperms are phanerogams: they bear seeds (naked on cones, not enclosed in fruit); 'no flower' doesn't mean 'no seed'.

options.text: None breaks it — seedless plants are always structurally simple and seedless equals non-vascular.
options.outcome: Pteridophytes falsify the equation directly: first terrestrial plants with vascular tissue, yet reproducing by spores.

c11_bio_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bio_ch04.scenario: At a marine museum's touch-tank exhibit you're asked to place mystery specimens into phylum bins using only symmetry, germ layers and coelom: a starfish (five arms, radial), a flatworm (bilateral, no body cavity), a roundworm (bilateral, cavity not fully lined by mesoderm) and an earthworm (segmented, true mesoderm-lined cavity). A volunteer assumes 'radial = simple diploblastic like jellyfish' and files the starfish with cnidarians.
c11_bio_ch04.prompt: Where did the filing go wrong?

options.text: The starfish is a triploblastic coelomate whose radial symmetry is secondary — adults radiate but the phylum sits with the coelomates (Echinodermata). Flatworm = triploblastic acoelomate, roundworm = pseudocoelomate, earthworm = coelomate; symmetry alone never fixes the phylum.
options.outcome: The three criteria act as a filter in sequence — symmetry, then germ layers, then coelom — and adult radial symmetry can sit on a fully triploblastic, coelomate body plan.

options.text: The volunteer is right — radial symmetry always pairs with diploblastic organisation.
options.outcome: Echinoderms are the standing counter-example: radial adults, triploblastic development, true coelom. One-to-one mapping between symmetry and germ layers is a memorisation shortcut, not a rule.

options.text: Flatworm and roundworm are interchangeable — bilateral means coelomate in both.
options.outcome: Bilateral triploblasts split three ways by cavity: flatworms acoelomate, roundworms pseudocoelomate, annelids onward coelomate — the cavity criterion does the separating.

c11_bio_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bio_ch05.scenario: Helping your grandmother sort vegetables for a school exhibition, you must label 'root vegetables' vs 'stem vegetables'. In the basket: carrot, radish, potato, ginger, onion. Your cousin sweeps all five into 'roots' — 'they all grow underground, case closed.'
c11_bio_ch05.prompt: Which ones are actually stems, and how do you prove it?

options.text: Potato, ginger and onion are stems: potato 'eyes' are nodes with axillary buds, ginger's rhizome has nodes, internodes and scale leaves, onion's bulb has a compressed stem base — roots never bear nodes or buds. Carrot and radish are true roots (from the radicle, no nodes, no buds).
options.outcome: Underground position is not a criterion; morphology — nodes, internodes, buds, scale leaves — and developmental origin decide root vs stem.

options.text: All five are roots — whatever grows below ground and stores food is by definition a root.
options.outcome: That rule misclassifies stem tubers, rhizomes and bulbs; a potato can sprout shoots from its nodes, something no root can do.

options.text: Potato is a root because it's tuberous like sweet potato — same shape, same organ.
options.outcome: Similar shape hides different origins: sweet potato is a modified root, potato a stem tuber — check for nodes ('eyes') to tell them apart.

c11_bio_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bio_ch06.scenario: The school gardener poses two puzzles to your biology group: 'My lawn gets mowed every week and regrows in days, but your desk-mate's rose bush, if cut to the ground, dies. Meanwhile my mango trunk gets fatter every year though no new tip forms.' A junior answers: 'Growth only happens at root and shoot tips — the grass must be growing from its tips that survived mowing.'
c11_bio_ch06.prompt: Which meristems explain the lawn and the mango trunk?

options.text: Lawn: intercalary meristems at the base of grass nodes keep dividing after the blade tips are cut — regrowth comes from the base, not the tip. Mango trunk: the lateral meristem (vascular cambium) adds secondary xylem and phloem each year, thickening the stem without any new tip.
options.outcome: Meristems aren't only apical — intercalary (nodes) and lateral (cambium) divisions explain regrowth-after-mowing and trunk thickening.

options.text: The junior is right — all plant growth is apical, so the grass tip must have survived under the soil.
options.outcome: If growth were purely apical, mown grass and a girdled trunk couldn't grow; intercalary and lateral meristems exist precisely where apical growth can't help.

options.text: The mango thickens because old cells keep dividing forever — permanent tissue can always revert to dividing.
options.outcome: Permanent tissues have lost division capacity; thickening comes from the vascular cambium, a dedicated lateral meristem — not from tired old cells reactivating.

c11_bio_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bio_ch07.scenario: During a hospital lab visit, a pathologist shows your group two slides: skin epidermis healing after a scrape, and trachea lining that looks 'stacked' under the microscope. A student says: 'In stratified skin epithelium the surface cells must divide to repair the scrape; and the trachea is clearly stratified too — the nuclei are at different levels.'
c11_bio_ch07.prompt: Which cells actually repair the skin, and is the trachea truly stratified?

options.text: Only the basal layer of the epidermis — the single row of cells touching the basement membrane — divides and pushes new cells upward; shed surface cells are terminally differentiated and cannot proliferate. The trachea is pseudostratified: nuclei at different heights, but every cell still contacts the basement membrane.
options.outcome: The basement-membrane-contact test separates true stratified epithelium (upper cells lose contact) from pseudostratified (all cells keep contact); repair capacity lives only in the basal layer.

options.text: Surface cells divide and reattach to heal the scrape — that's why skin heals fast.
options.outcome: Superficial cells are dead or anucleate and sloughing off; they can't divide — regeneration is the basal cells' job alone.

options.text: Trachea is truly stratified — nuclei at different levels prove stacked layers.
options.outcome: Staggered nuclei can fake stratification; trace each cell down — if every cell reaches the basement membrane it's pseudostratified, not stratified.

c11_bio_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bio_ch08.scenario: Your biology club is designing a 'life detector' badge for a science exhibition. A member writes the test as: 'Entity is living iff made of cells; viruses aren't made of cells, therefore viruses are simply non-living chemicals.' Another member says that's a circular definition, not a functional criterion.
c11_bio_ch08.prompt: What makes viruses exceptions to cell theory — in functional terms?

options.text: Viruses fail the functional test: no ribosomes (can't synthesise proteins), no mitochondria (can't make ATP), no independent metabolism or homeostasis, and no self-reproduction — they must hijack a host cell's machinery to replicate. 'Acellular' is the description; lack of metabolic autonomy is the reason.
options.outcome: Cell theory marks the cell as the smallest unit that can independently run all life processes — viruses are exceptions because they can't, not merely because they lack compartments.

options.text: The first member is right — 'made of cells' is the definition, so acellular means non-living; no further argument is needed.
options.outcome: That's circular: it names the boundary without explaining it — the theory's power is that the cell is the smallest independently functional unit.

options.text: Viruses are actually cells — just very small ones — so they follow cell theory like bacteria do.
options.outcome: Viruses have no cytoplasm, ribosomes or metabolic machinery; calling them tiny cells ignores why they can only replicate inside a host.

c11_bio_ch09.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bio_ch09.scenario: In the chemistry lab you're testing food extracts with Benedict's reagent for the science fair. A teammate predicts: 'Glucose and starch are both just glucose units, so both will give a strong brick-red precipitate; and once glucose is locked in a polymer, every anomeric carbon is consumed — no reducing ends remain.'
c11_bio_ch09.prompt: What will the test tubes actually show?

options.text: Glucose gives a strong positive. Starch/glycogen are only weakly reducing: every chain still carries ONE free anomeric carbon (the reducing end) — branching adds non-reducing ends but never removes the original. So polysaccharides can give a feeble positive, and after partial hydrolysis the signal strengthens as new reducing ends are generated.
options.outcome: Polymerisation doesn't consume all anomeric carbons; one reducing end per chain persists, which is why 'all polysaccharides are non-reducing' is wrong.

options.text: Starch will match glucose's strong positive — identical monomers mean identical chemistry.
options.outcome: Most anomeric carbons are locked in glycosidic bonds; only one reducing end per chain survives, so starch's Benedict's signal is feeble, not strong.

options.text: Polysaccharides are always non-reducing — polymerisation consumes every anomeric carbon in the chain.
options.outcome: Each chain keeps one free reducing end; α-1,6 branches create extra non-reducing ends but can't eliminate the original one.

c11_bio_ch10.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bio_ch10.scenario: For a biology practical you squash an onion root tip, stain with acetocarmine, and count 500 cells: 482 show a normal-looking nucleus with no visible chromosomes, 18 show condensed chromosomes in various mitotic stages. Your partner writes the conclusion: 'Root tip cells spend most of their time resting and occasionally divide.'
c11_bio_ch10.prompt: Is 'resting' the right word for what those 482 cells are doing?

options.text: No — those cells are in interphase, which your own count proves occupies >95% of the cycle. Far from resting: G1 builds proteins and organelles, S replicates the entire genome, G2 synthesises tubulin and checkpoint proteins. Interphase is the most metabolically intense stretch of the cycle.
options.outcome: The 'resting phase' label is a historical artefact — chromosomes are invisible then, so it looked idle; the cell is actually doing the heavy preparatory work.

options.text: Yes — the calm-looking nucleus without chromosomes means the cell is dormant between divisions.
options.outcome: Invisible chromosomes ≠ inactivity; that 'calm' nucleus is replicating billions of base pairs and building the machinery for mitosis.

options.text: Your count is biased — most cells are in mitosis but the stain missed them.
options.outcome: The stain marks condensed chromosomes reliably; the 96:4 ratio is exactly what theory predicts — interphase dominates because division is the short final act.

c11_bio_ch11.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bio_ch11.scenario: The school gardening club can afford one LED grow-light for the indoor spinach beds. The shop offers a cheap 'pure green' light ('leaves are green, so green is their colour') and a pricier blue+red dual-band light. A member says accessory pigments are just backup for damaged chlorophyll a, so a single peak is all that matters.
c11_bio_ch11.prompt: Which light actually powers growth, and why?

options.text: The blue+red light — chlorophyll a absorbs maximally at ~430 nm (blue) and ~662 nm (red), and accessory pigments (chlorophyll b, carotenoids) continuously harvest ~30% of incoming light at blue-green wavelengths and pass it to chlorophyll a by resonance transfer while quenching photo-oxidative damage. Green light is mostly reflected — that's why leaves look green.
options.outcome: Accessory pigments are always-on harvesters and protectors, not spares; feeding a plant the colour it reflects starves it.

options.text: The green light — leaves are green because they use green light most efficiently.
options.outcome: Green is reflected, not absorbed; absorption and action spectra both dip in the green band, so a green lamp photosynthesises poorly.

options.text: Either works — accessory pigments sit idle until chlorophyll a is damaged, so pigment variety doesn't change daily yield.
options.outcome: Accessory pigments transfer energy to the reaction centre every second the leaf is lit; removing their wavelengths cuts usable spectrum and removes protection from singlet oxygen.

c11_bio_ch12.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bio_ch12.scenario: After three days of heavy rain, the potted plants on your school's terrace garden start wilting even though the soil is soaked. A classmate explains: 'Roots can't respire because the leaves' stomata closed in the cloudy weather — the plant is suffocating from the top down.'
c11_bio_ch12.prompt: What's the real reason the roots are struggling?

options.text: Water fills the soil's air spaces, blocking O2 diffusion directly into root epidermal cells — roots get their oxygen from soil air (and via aerenchyma/lenticels in some plants), not shipped down from photosynthesis or through stomata. Saturated soil means hypoxic roots, whatever the leaves do.
options.outcome: Each plant part respires using locally available O2; the failure point in waterlogging is at the root surface, not the leaf.

options.text: The classmate is right — stomata are the plant's only breathing pores, so closed stomata starve the roots of oxygen.
options.outcome: Stomata serve leaves; stems use lenticels and roots absorb O2 from soil air spaces. Waterlogging kills by flooding those spaces, not by closing stomata.

options.text: Roots get O2 transported down through the phloem from photosynthesising leaves — cloudy skies cut off the supply.
options.outcome: Phloem carries sugars, not oxygen; root respiration depends on O2 diffusing from soil air into epidermal cells.

c11_bio_ch13.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bio_ch13.scenario: For a science exhibit you soak dry moong seeds and they visibly double in size overnight. Your partner logs this as 'growth' in the project notebook. Meanwhile a boiled (dead) seed placed in water also swells to the same size. The partner insists both are 'growing'.

options.text: No — swelling is imbibition, a reversible physical water uptake that even a dead seed shows. True growth is irreversible, metabolic, energy-dependent increase (cell division → elongation → maturation), starting only when the live seed's respiration and enzymes activate. Measure radicle length, not just diameter.
options.outcome: The live/dead pair is the perfect control: identical swelling in both proves the swelling itself isn't growth.

options.text: Both seeds are growing — any permanent-looking size increase counts as growth.
options.outcome: The dead seed can't grow — it has no metabolism; its swelling shows size increase alone doesn't imply growth. Also imbibition reverses on drying.

options.text: Only the live seed is growing — because its swelling is bigger.
options.outcome: Right conclusion, wrong reason: the distinction isn't amount but mechanism — metabolic, irreversible protoplasm increase versus passive water uptake.

c11_bio_ch14.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bio_ch14.scenario: Two neighbours fall ill in the same winter: one has bronchitis (inflamed bronchi) with a violent cough and mucus but normal blood oxygen; the other has pneumonia (inflamed alveoli) and turns dangerously hypoxic. Your friend is puzzled: 'Both are lung infections — why does only one starve the blood of oxygen?'
c11_bio_ch14.prompt: What structural fact explains the difference?

options.text: Gas exchange happens only in the respiratory zone — respiratory bronchioles and alveoli with simple squamous walls wrapped in pulmonary capillaries. The bronchi are conducting tubes (cartilage, ciliated epithelium, no capillaries): inflaming them causes cough and mucus but can't block diffusion; flooding the alveoli (pneumonia) directly attacks the exchange surface.
options.outcome: The conducting/exchange division of labour explains why same-organ diseases have different severity — location within the tree decides the functional hit.

options.text: Oxygen diffuses all along the bronchial tree, so bronchitis should cut oxygen just as much — the difference must be the germ.
options.outcome: Thick, cartilage-reinforced, ciliated bronchi have no capillaries to receive O2; diffusion is anatomically impossible there.

options.text: Pneumonia is worse only because it's a bigger infection area — any large bronchitis would drop oxygen equally.
options.outcome: Severity isn't about area inflamed but which histological zone is inflamed; even widespread bronchi can't exchange gas, while even partial alveolar flooding impairs it.

c11_bio_ch15.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bio_ch15.scenario: Your school hosts a blood-donation camp and a doctor shows smears explaining why a patient's report reads 'neutrophilia last week, lymphocytosis this week'. A volunteer explains to donors: 'All white cells fight infection the same way — they eat germs. T cells eat bacteria, B cells make the eating chemicals.'

options.text: Innate responders (neutrophils, monocytes) phagocytose fast — that's the early neutrophilia in acute bacterial infection. Adaptive lymphocytes don't engulf: B cells mature into plasma cells that secrete antibodies, T cells kill infected cells or activate other immune cells — explaining the later lymphocytosis in viral/chronic phases.
options.outcome: WBC types split into innate phagocytes and adaptive lymphocytes with distinct weapons; the differential count reads like an infection timeline.

options.text: The volunteer is right — every WBC fights by engulfing pathogens; the different names are just sizes.
options.outcome: Lymphocytes don't phagocytose at all; they run antibody production and cell-mediated killing — a different division of immune labour.

options.text: Close, but swapped: T cells make the antibodies and B cells do the eating.
options.outcome: Reversed — B cells (via plasma cells) secrete antibodies; T cells kill infected cells or coordinate the response; neither 'eats' bacteria like neutrophils do.

c11_bio_ch16.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bio_ch16.scenario: A hospital nephrology resident asks your internship group a puzzle: 'A rare disorder destroys only the juxtamedullary nephrons — about 15% of the total. Predict what the patient complains of.' A teammate shrugs: 'Losing 15% of filters just means 15% less filtration — mild problem.'
c11_bio_ch16.prompt: What does the patient actually suffer?

options.text: GFR falls only ~15%, but urine concentrating ability collapses: the deep medullary osmotic gradient is built solely by the long loops of Henle and vasa recta of juxtamedullary nephrons. The patient passes large volumes of dilute urine and dehydrates fast, even though 85% of nephrons still filter.
options.outcome: Cortical nephrons filter but can't build the gradient; the minority with long loops does the concentrating — losing them is a drought-tolerance disaster, not a filtration one.

options.text: The teammate is right — every nephron filters and concentrates equally, so 15% loss is a 15% loss.
options.outcome: Nephron labour is divided: ~85% are cortical with short loops that never reach the deep medulla; they can't substitute for the gradient-builders.

options.text: The patient can't filter blood at all — no juxtamedullary nephrons means no glomerular filtration.
options.outcome: Filtration happens in the cortical glomeruli of every nephron and continues fine; the deficit is in concentrating urine, not producing it.

c11_bio_ch17.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bio_ch17.scenario: In a physiology demo your teacher adds two drugs to separate cultures: cytochalasin D (blocks actin filaments) and colchicine (blocks microtubules). Your task: predict which stops (a) macrophages crawling to engulf debris, (b) tracheal cilia sweeping mucus, (c) a muscle fibre contracting. A classmate says all three involve 'beating or squeezing', so both drugs should stop everything.

options.text: Cytochalasin stops amoeboid crawling and muscle contraction (both actin/microfilament-based) but not cilia. Colchicine stops ciliary beating (9+2 microtubule axoneme powered by dynein) but not the actin systems. 'Beating' cilia and 'contracting' muscle run on entirely different molecular motors.
options.outcome: Matching movement to cytoskeleton — microfilaments for amoeboid/muscular, microtubules for ciliary — predicts the inhibitor correctly.

options.text: Both drugs stop all three — beating cilia are tiny muscles working by sliding filaments.
options.outcome: Cilia are microtubule-based with dynein motors, not actin-myosin; treating them as mini-muscles wrongly predicts they'll respond to actin blockers.

options.text: Colchicine stops everything because all movement needs ATP and microtubules.
options.outcome: All three use ATP, but macrophage pseudopodia and sarcomeres are actin-based; only cilia depend on microtubules.

c11_bio_ch18.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bio_ch18.scenario: You're building a model reflex-arc poster for the biology lab. For the sensory neuron you draw a unipolar cell from the dorsal root ganglion — one process, T-shaped. A teammate 'corrects' you: 'A unipolar neuron has only one process, so it can't have a dendrite. Redraw it so the signal enters through a proper branched dendrite tree.'
c11_bio_ch18.prompt: Who's right about where the sensory signal enters?

options.text: You are — in a unipolar sensory neuron the peripheral branch running to the skin receptor is functionally the dendrite: it receives the stimulus and conducts toward the cell body, even though it looks structurally axonal (myelinated, no Nissl's granules). Functional and structural classifications don't have to match.
options.outcome: The dorsal root ganglion neuron's single stem splits at a T-junction; the peripheral process plays the dendrite's role without the textbook branched look.

options.text: The teammate is right — one process means no dendrite, so the skin must synapse directly onto an axon that carries the signal to the cord.
options.outcome: There is no synapse at the receptor; the peripheral branch itself IS the receiving process — calling it 'not a dendrite' confuses structure with function.

options.text: Both wrong — unipolar neurons exist only in invertebrates; human sensory neurons are all multipolar.
options.outcome: Human dorsal root ganglion sensory neurons are the classic unipolar example; multipolar describes motor neurons and interneurons.

c11_bio_ch19.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bio_ch19.scenario: At a hospital's endocrine clinic you hear a doctor explain a patient's diabetes insipidus: 'His posterior pituitary isn't making enough ADH.' A medical intern corrects her notes, saying the posterior pituitary manufactures oxytocin and ADH just as the anterior lobe makes growth hormone.

options.text: No — ADH and oxytocin are synthesised in hypothalamic neuron cell bodies (supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei), travel down axons in the stalk, and are merely stored and released by the posterior pituitary. The anterior pituitary, in contrast, truly manufactures its tropic hormones under hypothalamic releasing/inhibiting hormone control via the portal blood.
options.outcome: Posterior pituitary = neural depot (stores hypothalamic hormones); anterior pituitary = true gland (makes its own under portal-vessel control).

options.text: Yes — whatever a gland releases, it must have synthesised; storage without synthesis isn't a gland's job.
options.outcome: The posterior pituitary is neural tissue, not glandular epithelium — a storage-and-release terminal for hypothalamic neurons.

options.text: Partly — the posterior pituitary makes ADH but the hypothalamus makes only the releasing hormones for the anterior lobe.
options.outcome: Hypothalamic neurons make BOTH the releasing/inhibiting factors for the anterior lobe and the finished ADH/oxytocin stored behind; splitting it that way misplaces the synthesis site.

c11_bs_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bs_ch01.scenario: Your commerce club is staging an exhibition on 'How Indian merchants paid each other in 1600'. One exhibit shows a Surat merchant who needs to pay a Calicut spice supplier. A teammate scripts it as: 'He loads gold coins on a bullock cart and hopes they arrive — India ran on barter before the British brought banking.'
c11_bs_ch01.prompt: Fix the script so it's historically accurate.

options.text: Show him issuing a Hundi — a negotiable credit instrument: his banker in Surat takes the money and writes a Hundi payable to the Calicut supplier, who presents it to a local banker for payment; the two bankers settle later through offsetting trade flows. No coins cross the country.
options.outcome: India had indigenous credit networks and instruments centuries before colonial rule; barter-and-coins undersells a system that made India a top global economy.

options.text: Keep the barter script — without banks, long-distance payment meant physically moving valuables or swapping goods.
options.outcome: The Hundi system solved exactly this problem: community-trust credit transfer between merchant-bankers, documented since early medieval inscriptions.

options.text: Have the merchant use a British-style bill of exchange — India's own instruments were too primitive for inter-city trade.
options.outcome: Hundi predates and parallels European bills; treating credit as a Western import erases a documented indigenous banking tradition.

c11_bs_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bs_ch02.scenario: Your friend's home bakery — a sole proprietorship — took a ₹6 lakh loan for ovens but the business is failing; bakery assets are worth only ₹2 lakh. The friend says: 'Worst case, they take the ovens and the shop — my family's flat and savings are safe because the loan belongs to the firm, which has unlimited liability.'
c11_bs_ch02.prompt: Is the family's personal property really safe?

options.text: No — unlimited liability attaches to the proprietor, not the firm: since business and owner are one legal entity, creditors can claim her personal assets (flat, car, savings) for the ₹4 lakh shortfall. That's the real price of total control and easy formation.
options.outcome: The phrase 'unlimited liability of the proprietor' means exactly that — personal wealth stands behind business debts.

options.text: Yes — 'unlimited liability of the firm' means the firm's own assets absorb any debt, however large; personal property is untouchable.
options.outcome: There's no separate firm to absorb anything — law sees no distinction between the bakery and its owner, so the shortfall reaches her personal assets.

options.text: Partly — personal assets are at risk only if she signed a personal guarantee; otherwise the firm's name shields her.
options.outcome: No guarantee is needed: in sole proprietorship there is no legal shield at all, guarantee or not — owner and business are the same person.

c11_bs_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bs_ch03.scenario: During a stock-market club session you're sorting enterprises for a mock ESG portfolio. Members argue over SAIL and BHEL: 'They say Ltd. and are Public Limited Companies whose shares trade on NSE — so they must be private sector. Public sector means something the public can't buy shares in, like the Railways.'
c11_bs_ch03.prompt: Which sector do SAIL and BHEL actually belong to?

options.text: Public sector — the test is ownership: government holds ≥51% of paid-up capital, making them Government Companies. 'Public Limited' only describes share transferability under the Companies Act; 'public sector' describes who owns it. SAIL is public limited by form and public sector by ownership.
options.outcome: Two different axes — legal form (public/private limited) and ownership (private individuals vs government ≥51%) — must not be conflated.

options.text: Private sector — anything listed on a stock exchange with 'Ltd.' in its name is a private company.
options.outcome: Exchange listing and 'Ltd.' are about form, not ownership; a company can be publicly traded AND government-owned.

options.text: Neither — if shares trade publicly it can't be 'public sector' because that term means closed to public participation.
options.outcome: 'Public' in public sector means owned by the public through government — the opposite of closed; citizens hold it via the state's majority stake.

c11_bs_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bs_ch04.scenario: Your startup club is pitching 'DabbaDash' — a service that collects home tiffins and delivers them to offices by lunch. An investor-judge asks: 'Why call this a service and not a goods business — you do move physical dabbas?' A teammate fumbles: 'Because it's fast and friendly.'
c11_bs_ch04.prompt: Give the investor the real answer using the five Is.

options.text: What's sold is the delivery performance, not the dabba: it's Intangible (can't be touched), Inconsistent (varies by route/rain), Inseparable (delivery happens as it's consumed), Inventory-less (today's unused slot can't be stored for tomorrow), and Involvement-heavy (customer must hand over the dabba and be reachable). The dabba is the customer's good; the transport-and-coordination is the service.
options.outcome: The five Is classify the offering by its nature — goods can be stored and standardised; this performance perishes if unused and is co-created with the customer.

options.text: It's a goods business — the customer receives a physical object (the delivered dabba), so tangibility wins.
options.outcome: The dabba belongs to the customer and is merely moved; what DabbaDash sells is the intangible, unstorable act of delivery — a service despite the goods involved.

options.text: 'Inconsistency' just means the service is low quality, and 'Inseparability' means customers can't switch providers.
options.outcome: Both misreadings matter: inconsistency is natural performance variability, not defect; inseparability is production-consumption simultaneity — the customer can still switch to a rival tomorrow.

c11_bs_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bs_ch05.scenario: Two neighbourhood bakeries compete in your school's 'digitisation challenge'. Bakery A builds a glossy website for online orders but keeps kitchen, stock and accounts on paper registers. Bakery B has no online shop at all, but its billing, inventory, production schedule and supplier ordering all run on one internal network. The judge asks which is the bigger e-business.
c11_bs_ch05.prompt: Which bakery is more of an e-business?

options.text: Bakery B — e-business covers every networked business function: intra-B coordination between sales, kitchen, inventory and accounts, plus B2B supplier ordering. A customer-facing website is only the B2C slice of e-commerce; Bakery A is a manual business with a digital brochure.
options.outcome: E-business is the firm's whole digital nervous system — internal networked processes count even with zero online sales.

options.text: Bakery A — e-business means selling online, and it has a storefront website while B doesn't sell to customers digitally at all.
options.outcome: That collapses e-business into B2C e-commerce; the NCERT definition covers industry, trade AND commerce over networks — including invisible internal processes.

options.text: Neither — e-business requires both online sales and internal networking, so both fail.
options.outcome: There's no such combined requirement; even a firm with no customer website can be an e-business if its internal functions run on networks (Intra-B).

c11_bs_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bs_ch06.scenario: Your friend's tiffin service legally uses single-use plastic boxes (the law doesn't ban them yet). She also pays her two delivery staff slightly below the legal minimum wage during a 'trial month', and plans a big Diwali donation to a temple as 'her social responsibility for the year'.
c11_bs_ch06.prompt: Sort her actions into legal, ethical and discretionary responsibility.

options.text: Below-minimum wages is illegal — not responsibility at all. Switching from plastic to reusable dabbas before the law forces it would be genuine social responsibility: voluntary, beyond compliance, with short-term cost. The temple donation is discretionary philanthropy — nice, but it doesn't offset legal or ethical failures.
options.outcome: Social responsibility starts where law ends; it isn't charity sprinkled over violations — fair wages are an obligation, not generosity.

options.text: The donation makes her socially responsible — giving back to society is exactly what the term means.
options.outcome: Charity is only the discretionary tip of responsibility; paying legal wages and not polluting are obligations that no donation can substitute for.

options.text: The trial-month wage cut is fine — she's a small business and social responsibility applies only to large corporates.
options.outcome: Minimum wage is legal responsibility, binding on every employer regardless of size; smallness exempts no one from law or ethics.

c11_bs_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bs_ch07.scenario: Three seniors plan to register 'CampusKart Pvt Ltd' to deliver stationery to hostels. Before incorporation, one of them signs a ₹60,000 contract with a supplier 'on behalf of the company', and they hire a CA to draft the MoA for a fee. Later they argue: 'The CA is a promoter since he helped form it, and the supplier contract automatically binds the company once it's registered.'
c11_bs_ch07.prompt: What does company law actually say?

options.text: The CA is not a promoter — professionals acting in their professional capacity are excluded by Section 69. And the pre-incorporation contract binds the signing promoter personally; the company can't ratify it because it didn't legally exist when the contract was made — a fresh contract is needed after incorporation.
options.outcome: Promotion is a defined legal phase: promoters carry fiduciary duty and personal liability until the company is born; helpers-for-fee are not promoters.

options.text: Both claims hold — anyone who helps form a company is a promoter, and contracts made for it get ratified at incorporation.
options.outcome: Section 69 expressly excludes professionals acting for a fee, and ratification is impossible — you can't adopt a contract on behalf of an entity that didn't exist.

options.text: The senior who signed is personally liable forever AND the company also owes the supplier — double liability.
options.outcome: The promoter is personally liable, but the company isn't bound at all until it makes a new contract post-incorporation — liability isn't duplicated.

c11_bs_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bs_ch08.scenario: Your entrepreneur club is budgeting a food-truck business: truck + kitchen fit-out ₹18 lakh, plus ₹4 lakh for fuel, ingredients and staff wages until revenue stabilises. A member proposes funding everything with a 90-day bank overdraft because 'finance is finance — just get the biggest loan you can'.
c11_bs_ch08.prompt: How should the ₹22 lakh actually be split and funded?

options.text: Match source to need: the ₹18 lakh is fixed capital (long-term, locked in the truck) best funded by long-term sources — owner's equity, long-term loan or lease; the ₹4 lakh is working capital (circulating, day-to-day) suited to short-term sources like overdraft or trade credit. A 90-day overdraft against an 8-year asset forces repayment long before the truck earns it back.
options.outcome: Every source sits on three axes at once — period, ownership, internal/external — and the funding horizon must match the asset's life.

options.text: One big overdraft is fine — a loan is a loan; you can always roll it over.
options.outcome: Short-term money funding a long-term asset creates a maturity mismatch: renewal risk, mounting interest and possible seizure mid-business.

options.text: Fund it all from owner's capital and retained earnings — borrowed funds are always dangerous.
options.outcome: Owners' funds and profits are legitimate internal sources, but ₹22 lakh from a student venture's own pocket is unrealistic — and retained earnings don't exist before the first profit.

c11_bs_ch09.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bs_ch09.scenario: Your uncle wants MSME benefits for his unit: investment in machinery ₹12 crore, annual turnover ₹8 crore. He insists it's 'Small' because turnover fits the Small band, while his accountant claims 'Micro' because... turnover is low. You must settle it before the Udyam registration.

options.text: Medium — the Act uses a dual threshold where BOTH limits must be met at each level: Micro fails (investment >₹1 cr), Small fails (investment >₹10 cr), Medium passes (≤₹50 cr investment AND ≤₹250 cr turnover). The first category where both criteria clear wins.
options.outcome: Neither 'turnover decides' nor 'higher capacity decides' — run the checks in ascending order and take the first band where both conditions pass.

options.text: Small — ₹8 crore turnover sits inside the Small band, and turnover reflects real activity better than sunk investment.
options.outcome: The dual test is a gate, not a preference: ₹12 cr investment breaks Small's ₹10 cr investment ceiling, so the unit can't be Small whatever its turnover.

options.text: Micro — smaller turnover should pull the classification down to the lowest qualifying label.
options.outcome: There's no 'pulling down' to a band whose limits are breached; Micro needs investment ≤₹1 cr, which ₹12 cr fails outright.

c11_bs_ch10.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bs_ch10.scenario: In a business-studies quiz bowl you're asked to sort four trades: (a) a Punjab farmer sells wheat to a Punjab mill, (b) the mill sells flour to a Delhi wholesaler, (c) the wholesaler sells to a Kochi retailer, (d) a Surat firm ships spices to Dubai. A rival buzzes: '(b) and (c) are external trade — they cross state borders.'
c11_bs_ch10.prompt: Which trades are internal, which external?

options.text: (a), (b) and (c) are all internal trade — the border that matters is the national one, not state lines; no customs duty applies anywhere inside India. Only (d) is external/international because goods cross the national frontier into the UAE.
options.outcome: Internal trade means buyer and seller both within the country's boundaries — distance and state lines are irrelevant.

options.text: The rival is right — 'internal' means within a state, so inter-state commerce is external.
options.outcome: That uses the everyday meaning of 'internal'; the trade definition turns on national borders — inter-state sales remain domestic internal trade.

options.text: (a) isn't trade at all — a village farmer selling at a mandi is informal, not 'trade'.
options.outcome: Formality isn't the criterion either; a farmer's mandi sale is a genuine internal wholesale transaction feeding the distribution chain.

c11_bs_ch11.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bs_ch11.scenario: At a career talk, a student claims: 'International business is only for firms that ship physical goods abroad — Infosys writing software for American banks, Pepsi licensing its syrup formula to a Thai bottler, and Tata buying a stake in a Kenyan tea estate don't count, because nothing crosses a border in a container.'

options.text: No — international business includes every commercial activity across national frontiers: services exports (Infosys), licensing/franchising of intellectual property (Pepsi), foreign investment (Tata's stake), contract manufacturing, and movement of capital, personnel and technology — not just merchandise in containers.
options.outcome: Trade in goods is only one component; the invisible flows of services, IP and capital are equally international business.

options.text: Yes — 'business across borders' requires goods to physically cross; services and licences are domestic knowledge work.
options.outcome: That confuses international trade (merchandise) with the broader international business, which the definition extends to services, capital, technology and IP.

options.text: Half right — services count as international business only if the worker physically travels abroad.
options.outcome: Personnel movement is one component, but cross-border service delivery happens electronically too — an Indian firm billing a US client from Bengaluru is international business.

c11_chem_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c11_chem_ch01.scenario: A wellness stall at your school fair sells '100% chemical-free' fruit juice and 'all-natural' detergent. A classmate wants to buy the juice, saying: 'At least this one has no chemicals — chemistry is lab stuff, I don't want it in my food.'

options.text: Everything is chemistry — the juice is water, sugars, vitamins, acids; 'natural' vitamin C and lab-made vitamin C are the same molecule. The label confuses 'chemical' (everything made of atoms) with 'synthetic additive'. Chemistry isn't confined to labs: the juice's preservation, the detergent's surfactants, even your saliva are molecular processes.
options.outcome: Chemistry is the study of matter's composition and transformations — you can't buy your way out of it; 'chemical-free' would mean a vacuum.

options.text: The label is honest — natural juice has no chemicals because chemicals are artificial substances made in labs.
options.outcome: That splits the world into 'natural = safe' and 'chemical = artificial'; glucose from an orange and glucose synthesised in a factory are identical molecules.

options.text: It means 'free of harmful chemicals' — so the claim is scientifically fine, just informal.
options.outcome: Even read charitably, 'harmful' depends on dose and identity, not origin — the claim still trades on a meaningless word; every ingredient in the bottle is a chemical.

c11_chem_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c11_chem_ch02.scenario: In the physics-chemistry lab your teacher brings a discharge tube and a bar magnet. The glowing beam bends when the magnet approaches and drifts toward the positive plate of an electric field. A student objects: 'It's just a ray like light — it travels straight and makes things glow, so it's an electromagnetic wave, not particles.'

options.text: Deflection by electric and magnetic fields — EM waves are electrically neutral and can't be bent by a field; only a stream of charged particles (electrons, negative) responds, curving toward the positive plate. Straight-line travel and fluorescence are shared with light, but field deflection is exclusively particle behaviour.
options.outcome: Same shadow-casting, opposite physics: the beam's response to fields was the decisive evidence that cathode rays are charged matter, not radiation.

options.text: The straight-line travel and sharp shadows — only waves can do that, so it must be light-like.
options.outcome: Particles moving fast also travel straight and cast shadows; the test that separates waves from particles is field deflection, which this beam fails the 'wave' prediction on.

options.text: Neither — you can't tell particles from waves in a school lab at all.
options.outcome: A magnet and a charged plate are exactly the apparatus that settled it historically; school-lab deflection reproduces Thomson's evidence directly.

c11_chem_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c11_chem_ch03.scenario: For a chemistry-day exhibit your team rebuilds Mendeleev's card-sorting method: each card carries an element's atomic weight plus its oxide and hydride formulae. Sorting by weight puts tellurium (127.6) before iodine (126.9) — but Te's compounds look like sulphur's family while iodine's look like chlorine's. A member insists: 'Atomic weight is the law; never swap the order.'
c11_chem_ch03.prompt: What did Mendeleev actually do here?

options.text: He inverted them — placing Te in Group VI with S/Se and iodine in Group VII with Cl/Br — because chemical behaviour (valency, compound formulae) was his primary classifier and atomic weight only the ordering aid. The same inversions (Ar/K, Co/Ni) exposed the limit of weight-based ordering and pointed toward atomic number.
options.outcome: Mendeleev's genius was trusting chemistry over arithmetic; the 'anomalous pairs' later became evidence that atomic number, not weight, is the real ordering parameter.

options.text: The member is right — periodic law means strict weight order, so Te stays before I even if properties mismatch.
options.outcome: That misreads the law: Mendeleev broke weight order whenever chemistry demanded it — properties were the function, weight just the rough index.

options.text: Leave both out of the table — elements that don't fit the order get discarded.
options.outcome: Mendeleev did the opposite: he left deliberate gaps for unknown elements (eka-aluminium, eka-silicon) but never dropped a known one for misbehaving.

c11_chem_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c11_chem_ch04.scenario: In a peer-tutoring session you ask juniors to draw Lewis structures for BF3, NO2 and SF6. One junior forces five bonds onto nitrogen 'to complete its octet', refuses SF6 entirely ('sulphur can't have twelve electrons — octet rule!'), and concludes BF3 must be wrongly described by chemists.
c11_chem_ch04.prompt: How do you correct the session?

options.text: The octet rule is a guide with three known failure modes: incomplete octet (BF3 — boron stable at 6 e⁻), odd-electron species (NO2 — one atom keeps 7 e⁻), and expanded octet (SF6 — period-3+ atoms can exceed 8). Forcing octets everywhere produces impossible structures like pentavalent N.
options.outcome: Formal charge and total valence count pick the best Lewis structure; period-2 atoms are octet-bound, but the rule bends below and beyond.
